description: Three example 'tasks at hand'. Each task lists the fragments (by doc file + frag id) and telemetry that matter for it, with a weight and a one-line why. This file IS the 'fake smart part' for the front-end assignment: a candidate's app can read it directly instead of building any real relevance logic. Weights: critical = miss this and you will likely build something wrong or break something; helpful = makes the work better/faster; background = context, fine to dim or collapse.

tasks.title: Bring back saved cards at checkout
tasks.story: Roadmap Bet 1. A developer (or coding agent) is about to design and build saved cards. The catch: the most detailed document about saved cards is abandoned and partly wrong, and the real constraints are scattered across payments, fraud, security, and an incident report.

fragments.why: The only allowed storage approach today: provider tokens, never card numbers. Directly contradicts the abandoned PRD.
The trap itself: the most findable saved-cards doc proposes a storage design that is now forbidden. Surfacing it WITH its warning is the whole game.
Any new charge path must reuse attempt IDs on retry; saved-card charges are a new charge path.
Saved card + new device + >Rs.2000 goes to review before capture; the checkout flow must design for a 'confirming payment' state.
Hold at checkout, capture after weighing — saved cards change how the card is entered, not when money moves.
The customer research and checkout UX from the abandoned PRD are still valid and save redoing the research.
The story behind the attempt-ID rule; makes the rule stick.
Saved-card orders with weighed items still hold 120% and capture must never exceed the hold.
Every surface showing a saved card is last-4 + network only; support tooling included.
Cards have no backup provider and manual recharges are forbidden — shapes error handling for saved-card failures.
Why this task exists and its priority.
Amounts on any new payment path are integer paise.

telemetry.why: The quantitative case: typed cards fail first attempt at 9.1% vs 2.8% provider benchmark for saved tokens; plus the 38s checkout gap and 12% card-entry abandonment.
telemetry.chart_idea: Typed-card vs saved-token first-attempt failure rate, and the weekly typed-card trend.

tasks.title: Evaluate a wider delivery window for Indore
tasks.story: Leadership decided in Nov 2025 to keep the two-hour promise and fix Indore capacity instead. A developer (or agent) asked to 'look into a 4-hour option for Indore' must first discover that this exact debate already happened, what was decided and why, and which systems quietly assume 90 minutes.

fragments.why: The decision and its reasoning already exist. Any work here starts from this, not from zero — and the allowed shape is 'scheduled option beside the promise', never a replacement.
The real time budget: 5 min store window + 90 min plan + ~25 min buffer. 'Four hours' touches all three numbers, not one.
Batching logic hard-assumes the 90-minute plan; a window change means rework, not a config edit.
Indore stores close at 9 pm — a wider evening window may promise hours that physically cannot exist.
Customer clock vs ops clock differ by up to 5 minutes; any lateness analysis must state which clock it uses.
The 5-minute window is contractual; no product change can reclaim it.
The root cause is rider capacity, seasonal in Indore — the thing the decision chose to fix instead.
The tested ceiling a wider window would tempt people to raise; raising it means retesting.
Indore demand spikes sharply in festival weeks while rider supply dips.
Where the customer clock starts in the order lifecycle.
Later deliveries interact with quiet hours; only 'rider arriving' may go out at night.

telemetry.why: Indore at 84.2% on-time vs 96.2% Pune, with the pain concentrated 5-8 pm — the evidence that started the debate, and the numbers any fix must move.
telemetry.chart_idea: On-time rate by city, and Indore's by-hour dip.

tasks.title: Make substitution suggestions automatic and smarter
tasks.story: Roadmap Bet 2. A developer (or agent) is about to build automatic substitute suggestions. The rules that must not be broken live in the spec; the reality that must be respected lives in picker notes and incident history; and two payment rules silently constrain which substitutes are even allowed per order.

fragments.why: The absolute line: never across veg/non-veg, baby food, or allergy items. No model or experiment may relax it.
The offer order (size swap, then brand swap, then nothing) is fixed; 'smarter' means better candidates within the ladder.
UPI orders may only get equal-or-cheaper substitutes — the candidate set depends on payment method, which almost everyone misses.
The picker is the sensor; flows that make pickers argue with the database get worked around within a week.
Substitute mappings must key on listing_uid; store item codes get reused and will silently corrupt mappings.
Stock data is a 30-minute-old hint that can fail while looking healthy; suggestions must degrade gracefully.
The 110% price cap, and why it fits inside the 120% card hold.
Three minutes is all the plan affords; 22% of prompts already time out to defaults.
Substituting weighed items re-enters the weighing flow; prices are estimates until the scale.
Wrong substitutes are the top human-handled complaint — the metric this work should move.
Why substitution is a core flow: stock can fail while looking healthy, and the product must degrade gracefully.
The cultural one-liner behind all of it — from a stale, unowned doc, which is itself a trust signal to convey.
Cheaper substitutes on UPI turn into automatic credits under Rs.100.

telemetry.why: Acceptance by category and swap type (size swaps beat brand swaps everywhere; baby care barely accepts at all), and where OOS actually happens (evening vegetables).
telemetry.chart_idea: Acceptance rate by category split by swap type; morning vs evening OOS by category.

telemetry.why: The cost of getting it wrong today: 9,140 unwanted-substitute refunds a month, 41 broken-rule flags.
